questions.title: What is the exact role of the two-step reasoning instruction in FeatLLM's prompt?
questions.question_body: In the FeatLLM paper, the authors describe a ‘Reasoning instruction’ that splits the LLM’s inference into a first step of inferring causal relationships without demonstrations, and a second step using demonstrations to derive rules. I am unclear why this separate two-step is necessary. Wouldn’t a single chain-of-thought prompt that includes demonstrations be sufficient? How does the separation affect the LLM’s ability to avoid spurious correlations, and what evidence do the authors provide that this improves rule quality?

questions.title: How does FeatLLM handle opaque or noisy rule outputs from the LLM?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that LLMs may use slightly different phrasing for inequalities (e.g., "greater than" vs. ">") and that parsing these rules automatically is challenging. They propose feeding the rules back into the LLM as a code generation task. Could someone walk me through an example of how this parsing prompt is constructed? Specifically, how does it ensure that the generated Python code correctly implements the rule even if the natural language contains synonyms or misspellings?

questions.title: Why are rules represented as binary features rather than continuous scores?
questions.question_body: FeatLLM creates new binary features by checking whether each rule holds for a sample, then learns weights for these binary features. I wonder whether treating each rule as a hard 0/1 indicator is necessary. Would allowing soft values (e.g., probability that a rule is satisfied) improve learning, especially when less than 10 true examples exist? What trade-offs did the authors consider in choosing hard binary features?

questions.title: How does bagging mitigate prompt size limits in FeatLLM?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that bagging allows FeatLLM to handle tabular datasets with many features by limiting prompt length per LLM call. I would appreciate a concrete explanation: when bagging, which elements are subsampled – columns, rows, or both? How many samples or columns are typically kept to stay within GPT-3.5's token limit? Does bagging affect which rules are extracted and how ensemble averaging compensates?

questions.title: What happens if a feature type mismatch occurs during rule generation?
questions.question_body: In the prompt design section it says that when formulating rules, they let the LLM refer to feature type in basic info to avoid type mismatches. However, I still see some generated rules referring to numeric comparisons on categorical variables or vice versa. How robust is FeatLLM to such mistakes? Does it throw an error in parsing or simply ignore those rules?

questions.title: How sensitive is FeatLLM to the number of rules per class?
questions.question_body: The paper fixes 10 rules per class and performs an ablation study on this parameter. For datasets with many classes (e.g., 4 or more), does generating a fixed number of rules per class cause imbalanced representation of classes? Would it make sense to adjust the number of rules proportional to class frequency or sample size?

questions.title: What is the justification for applying a ReLU-like maximum on weights in Eq. (1)?
questions.question_body: $w_k$ are trained weights applied to binary rule features, and they project them into non‑negative space using $	ext{max}(w_k,0)$. Why not allow negative weights? How does enforcing non‑negativity help with interpretability or prevent negative influence from noisy rules?

questions.title: "Information gain" vs "Feature usefulness" in measuring rule quality
questions.question_body: "Quality of features" experiment averages AUROC between each new rule feature and target label before and after tuning. Is AUROC an appropriate metric for assessing rule usefulness? Would mutual information or Gini impurity provide better insights given these are binary features?

questions.title: How does FeatLLM compare against fine‑tuned LLMs like TabLLM when using zero‑shot versus few‑shot prompts?
questions.question_body: "FeatsLLM" only needs API access and no fine‑tuning, whereas TabLLM requires parameter-efficient tuning (IA3) which still demands loading checkpoints. In practice, could we achieve similar performance by simply increasing temperature or temperature–top‑p sampling without tuning? How do we quantify relative efficiency between these approaches beyond inference cost?

questions.title: "Effect of adding spurious correlations" experiment interpretation
questions.question_body: "They attach irrelevant columns from Adult dataset to Heart data" – how exactly was relevance determined? Was there any control where correlated but truly informative columns were added? How might one distinguish between random noise and genuine but misleading correlations in practice when evaluating FeatLLM’s robustness?

questions.title: "Feature bagging" strategy details
questions.question_body: "Feature bagging" is mentioned as part of ensemble; however, unlike random forests where bagging uses bootstrap sampling of instances and subset of features for each tree, FeatLLM’s bagging seems different. What sampling scheme exactly is used: number of instances sampled per trial, number of features considered per trial? Are there hyper‑parameters governing this sampling strategy?
